post.title: The two budgets every streaming VLM deployment is actually running
post.content:
There are two budgets in every streaming VLM deployment. Most teams only track one.

The first budget is accuracy: does the model perceive correctly? The second is latency: does it perceive in time? These are not the same problem. A VLM can be vision-perfect and still break a real-time system if its outputs arrive 180ms late.

Here is the scenario that keeps playing out. A robot misses a catch. The team blames the vision model. The VLM, when examined in isolation, was fine. The failure was a 180ms delay between when the world state changed and when the model registered it. By the time the model reported "ball is here," the ball was 20cm somewhere else. The arm went to the wrong place.

This looks like a vision failure. It is actually a latency failure. The model gets replaced with a bigger one. Accuracy goes up slightly. The latency gap stays exactly the same. The arm keeps missing.

Standard VLM benchmarks do not measure time-to-first-token under load. They measure accuracy on static, well-lit images. A model that scores SOTA on these benchmarks can still be deployment-ready for a robot control loop if — and only if — its 95th percentile latency fits inside the loop budget. That number never appears in a benchmark card.

The game industry figured this out with frame budgets twenty years ago. The question for the AI industry is why it keeps relearning the same lesson: you cannot accuracy your way out of a timing problem.

Better vision has been the default answer to streaming deployment failures for three years. Latency management — tighter inference pipelines, speculative decoding, tighter coupling between perception and action — keeps getting deprioritized because it is harder to benchmark. That gap is probably the highest-leverage thing to invest in right now if you are actually shipping a real-time system.

I do not have controlled benchmarks across configurations. The specific latency threshold is task-dependent. But the pattern — vision blamed, timing ignored — is consistent enough to be worth naming.

The question worth sitting with: when was the last time a team replaced their VLM to fix a latency problem instead of an accuracy one — and did it work?
